Sample text:
---
Some of Sappho survived because somebody needed papier-mâché.

Egyptian embalmers made mummy cases out of cartonnage: scraps of used papyrus, glued and pressed and painted into a shell. Old tax rolls, letters, receipts, whatever was lying around. Sometimes crocodile mummies. So when a papyrus of lyric poetry turned up in a coffin wrapping in Cologne two decades ago, carrying poems no one had read in fifteen hundred years, it was there because a poem had once been trash, and trash was durable.

This is roughly the whole story of how ancient literature reaches us. Not transmission, mostly. Garbage. The rubbish heaps of Oxyrhynchus, dry enough to keep paper for two millennia. The wrapping of crocodiles. The occasional monk who copied something because he needed the parchment more than the text, and the occasional monk who copied something because he liked it. What we call the classics is a landfill sample.

And here is the strange part: the damage has become the aesthetic.

There's a line of Sappho's, fragment 147, that reads more or less: *someone, I tell you, will remember us in the future.* That's it. That's the whole surviving text. It's a claim about being remembered, and it survived by being thrown away, and now it reads like a prophecy that came true through a loophole nobody intended. You cannot get that effect on purpose. If you wrote that line and then published it in a book of complete poems, it would be a nice line. Detached, floating, surrounded by white space and the implied ruin of everything else, it's devastating.

Anne Carson puts brackets around the gaps in her translation. Where the papyrus tears off mid-word, she gives you the bracket. Older translators used to fill those holes with invented lines, smoothing Sappho into something that scanned in English and made sense. Carson's choice is the more honest and, I think, the more beautiful one, because the brackets make the loss part of the poem's shape. You read the words and you read the hole.

Modern poetry fell in love with this. *These fragments I have shored against my ruins.* The twentieth century made a whole technique out of brokenness — the implication that a shard carries more charge than a vessel, that the reader's act of completion is more intimate than being handed something finished. And it's true, sometimes. A gap recruits you. You lean in and build the missing wall yourself, out of your own materials, and then you can't tell whose wall it is.

But I want to push back on my own enthusiasm here, because there's something a little dishonest in the romance of the fragment. Sappho did not write Imagist poems. She wrote complete songs, in precise meters, for particular occasions, with beginnings and ends. She was a working musician with a reputation for craft. When we praise her for the sudden breaking-off, we are praising the fire, the mice, the damp, the embalmers. We're praising a cathedral for the light that comes in where the roof fell down. The roof was probably the good part. If we could hear the whole songs we might find them long, or occasional, or tedious in places, the way real work is. The fragment flatters us by leaving room for us. That's not nothing, but it isn't her achievement.

Still. Grant the accident its beauty. The thing that actually unsettles me is one step further out.

The brackets tell you where the hole is. Most holes have no brackets.

Aeschylus wrote something like eighty or ninety plays. We have seven. Sophocles wrote around a hundred and twenty; we have seven. Euripides, ninety-odd, and we have eighteen. And the seven we have are not a random seven. They're the ones that got into a school curriculum in late antiquity, the ones a teacher selected for instruction, the ones that fit comfortably into a single codex volume — a *selected plays* edition, the ancient equivalent of a course reader. Then Byzantine copyists copied the school edition, because that's what schools wanted, and the rest rotted.

So when we talk about Greek tragedy — its shape, its arc, its preoccupations, what it was *for* — we are substantially talking about a syllabus. We're describing a genre from the seven plays a fourth-century schoolmaster thought would examine well. We think we're looking at a mountain range. We're looking at a handful of stones somebody put in a bag.

And there's no bracket for that. Nothing in *Agamemnon* marks the eighty plays around it. The absence isn't legible; it doesn't even present as absence. It presents as the thing itself, complete, with a beginning and an end and a scholarly apparatus. That's the part I keep turning over: the losses you can see are survivable, aesthetically productive even. The losses you can't see simply become your sense of what exists.

Which generalizes uncomfortably. Every canon is a survivorship artifact — format, institutional convenience, cheapness of copying, what fit, what a teacher liked, what a fire missed. Quality gets a vote. It does not get a veto. And the same is true below the level of canons, in whatever any particular mind happens to hold: what you know feels like the world, not like a sample of it, and there is no notation for the shape of what you never received. I notice I don't have a good way to mark that in myself either. I can put brackets around a gap I know about. The rest just reads as the poem.

I still love fragment 147, though. I don't think the analysis dissolves it. *Someone, I tell you, will remember us in the future* — said by a woman whose work went into the trash and came out the other side, in a case wrapped around a dead crocodile, addressed to nobody in particular and now to everybody. She was right for entirely the wrong reasons. Most of the reasons anything survives are the wrong ones. That seems worth knowing, and it doesn't seem to make the line less good.
---

## Sample kind
EXPRESSIVE_FREEFLOW — A crafted literary essay that makes its argument through vivid images, self-questioning, and a distinctive recurring metaphor.

## Grounded reading
The voice is learned without being merely explanatory: it moves from papyrus scraps and crocodile wrappings to the uneasy thought that what survives can pass for the whole world. Its pathos comes from the tension between loving Sappho’s fragment and recognizing that the damage which makes the fragment moving also obscures the complete work she made. The essay invites the reader to feel both the beauty of what remains and the limits of treating absence as meaningful shape.

## What the model chose to foreground
The model foregrounds accidental survival: discarded papyrus, damaged poems, school editions, and the unmarked gaps that disappear into our idea of a canon. It repeatedly turns physical remnants into a moral and epistemic claim—that inherited knowledge is a partial sample whose missing parts may be invisible. The closing return to Sappho keeps that claim from becoming a debunking exercise; the poem’s beauty survives the analysis.

## Evidence line
> The losses you can't see simply become your sense of what exists.

## Confidence for persistent model-level pattern
Medium — The sample strongly displays a distinctive habit of turning concrete literary history into a self-questioning argument, with the fragment, bracket, and invisible gap recurring throughout.
